en: **The Śrī-Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Stotra: The Garland of Twenty-Four Verses** I meditate upon that Inner Self (Pratyagātman) who is the southern face [of Śiva], whose name "Om" is grasped by the wise, and by whose light all this—beginning with the ether—is illumined; and from whom, when unknown, the gods headed by Brahmā remain fixed in their respective positions. 1.

To that Lord whose lotus-feet grant the goals of human existence swiftly to those who bow with devotion and destroy all their calamities; to Him who, for the sake of destroying delusion, possesses the flute, the seal of consciousness, the bow, the lute, the eyes, and the rosary, [and who is preceded by the disciples of the Flautist and the Son of Vyāsa]... 2.

They worship that Lord, who is mounted upon a noble elephant, who bestows auspiciousness upon his devotees, and who is served by those who have propitiated him with their lotus-like hands; they bow down to that ocean of compassion, whom the Ādityas seek for the fulfillment of their desires.

...those beings dwelling within the womb, terrified of the exceedingly vast ocean of worldly existence, find refuge in him who is intent on severing the bonds of existence; those fortunate ones whose faces possess the luster of the full moon worship his feet, which are like a pair of shimmering lotuses. 5–6.
They serve him who sits at the foot of the banyan tree, infinite...

(6) He, by whose beautiful masses of splendor—arising from the sun-gems set in his armlets and illuminating the entire world—the elements beginning with ether, air, fire, and water [are sustained] as the embodiment of light... (7)
Having abandoned all rituals involving substances such as curd and clarified butter, he here cultivates a longing for the fruits of action;
that god upon earth whom the seeker of the fruit in the form of spiritual inquiry [approaches]—[him...
8 ...whom one of great merit, worshipping in this world, quickly becomes free from mental affliction and has cast off all the sufferings of worldly existence.

...Him whom those devoted ones rejoice in, having attained all the Vedas and Tantras, as they recite at the proper time the mantra consisting of the syllables situated between *na* and *ma*, which is the supreme Brahman that has become the inner self (pratyag-bhūta) and is the eternal sacrifice (satra). 9–10.
...him whose laughter, surpassing the Mandākinī, the kunda flowers, the mass of frost, the ocean, nectar, and the celestial elephant, is as white as a cloud;
him who possesses the river of the gods (the Gaṅgā) shining with waves and ripples rising from the cauldron of his matted locks that have the luster of molten gold. 11–12.
Him who is eternal, subtle, and eternally free from all defects... (12) By the knowledge of whom alone everything becomes known, since any other entity in the world is like a hare's horn;
for those who have attained Him, there is nothing further to be attained—Him, who is without beginning... (13)

Māra, whose body was reduced to ashes by the flashing bolts of fire born from the eye on his forehead, became the fine incense powder for him... (14) For those wallowing in the ocean of Saṃbhū, which is the nature of saṃsāra, devotion to his feet is the sturdy ship to reach its further shore... (15)
...him, who is to be propitiated by all, the ocean of bliss pervading all—[he] would become wise.

Meditating in his heart upon his form for even half a blink of an eye—one who wears the moon as an ornament, holds a lute, has the luster of camphor, carries a book in his hand, and has lotus-like eyes—he [would become wise]. 15–16.

He who is the supreme abode of grains and of those things possessing mature radiance such as the sun and others; he who is the cause of the origin of the universe and so forth; he whose [servants] are all these others—he is that Lord of All, worthy of praise... (17) ...by devotees capable of withdrawal of the senses, restraint of breath, and so forth, who are self-controlled yet strive even with unsteady minds.
He who is known with speed as one's very own self...

18 The Lord, residing within the mind, impels these living beings—who have become portions of His knowledge—toward all their various duties; He does so while conforming to their past karma, [bestowing] that fruit upon them. 19

The wise, who have realized the truth through experience, declare Him to be pure wisdom, the one who has attained self-awareness, the beloved of His own devotees, the impeller of the vital breath, the senses, and so forth, and the meaning of the syllable *praṇava*—Him whom they describe...
(20). Through the knowledge of Him alone does the understanding of the cycle of worldly existence arise for men, and through the knowledge of Him alone does liberation occur.
[He] clearly speaks of that primordial Teacher of the Vedas...
(21) In whom the tree of ignorance has been severed, and with it the universe superimposed upon him—including even this distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme Lord;
who, like the sun among its rays or water in a vessel, is free from all duality—him [I worship]. (22)
Neither sleep, nor dreaming, nor even the waking state exists there; nor is the all-pervading vital breath (prāṇa) present, for he is the Self of all.
He who is the immutable, the absolute essence of pure consciousness and bliss—[bow to] him...
23. "Alas! Alas! thus did the foremost sages express their amazement upon realizing that when he is known as one's own Self, there is no longer delusion regarding the self.
How can he [the Supreme Self] be thus [perceived] when He has entered into Brahman as the inner self?

24 May that Sovereign of Teachers, the Supreme Self, who is gracious and skillful, out of compassion remove this very [obscuration] which was initially concealed by beautiful meters called *mattamayūra* and by the artful arrangement of syllables and words. 25
Thus ends the Dakṣiṇāmūrtivarṇamālāstotra composed by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya.
